Overall concept quality: moderate-to-weak as presented, though the underlying problem space is real and worthwhile.

Strengths: (1) The core problem is genuine and well documented in the broader world: shift-work fatigue drives accidents, health problems, and lost productivity, so the pain category is credible. (2) The team identifies a plausible workflow gap: occupational clinics largely rely on self-reported 'fine or not fine' sleep assessments, and combining sleep logs with shift schedules is a sensible, differentiated data framing versus generic consumer sleep trackers. (3) Targeting clinics as an initial B2B channel is more defensible than going direct to consumers. (4) A working MVP exists.

Weaknesses: (1) The pain is asserted, not validated. There is no evidence that occupational clinics actually experience this as a pressing, budgeted problem, no customer interviews, no pilot, and the only feedback is friends and family saying it 'looks good.' It is unclear whether clinics want this data, would change behavior because of it, or would pay for it. The person with the pain (the tired worker) is not the buyer, and the buyer (the clinic) has no demonstrated urgency. (2) The solution is thin and not clearly compelling. Manual self-entry of sleep times via a website is high-friction, low-compliance, and less accurate than passive wearable data that already exists; it is unclear why tired shift workers would consistently log data, or why the clinic benefits beyond what a simple sleep diary already provides. The 'score' and 'analytics' are undefined, with no scientific or clinical validation, and the claim of a 'holistic end to end solution' is marketing language rather than substance. (3) Uniqueness is overstated. The claim of being 'first to this niche' rests on a self-admittedly cursory competitor search. Fatigue risk management is an established field with existing products and fatigue-modeling tools in transportation, healthcare, and safety, and wearables firms and employer wellness platforms could easily add schedule integration. No defensible moat (proprietary data, clinical validation, integrations, distribution) is identified. (4) The business model is undefined: it is unclear who pays (clinic, worker, employer, data buyers), at what price, and why. Selling worker health data is also a red flag. (5) Clinical credibility is absent: no clinician or sleep expert on the team, and the product generates health recommendations and 'rest plans' with unaddressed regulatory and privacy exposure (HIPAA, potential FDA considerations, liability). (6) The value proposition lacks a clear outcome claim, such as fewer incidents, better clinical decisions, or lower costs, that would make the product compelling to a buyer.

Verdict: The idea targets a real problem area and shows reasonable founder intuition, but the offering is currently an unvalidated hypothesis with a low-differentiation, high-friction solution and no evidence of a clearly identified buyer need. To become compelling, the team would need customer discovery with clinics, a defined buyer and value metric, clinical advisory input, a differentiated data or workflow advantage, and a pilot demonstrating that clinicians actually use the output to change patient care.

Business plan text:

Sleepledger
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Sleepledger, Inc. (S Corp)
The Problem
Shift workers do not sleep good. This is a well known problem that effects millions of workers
across America and the world. Nurses work night shifts, truck drivers drive at all hours,
factory workers rotate between days and nights, and all of them have fatigue. Fatigue can lead
to accidents, mistakes, health problems, and lower productivity. Occupational clinics, which
are the clinics that see workers for work related health matters, do not have a good way to
know how their patients are sleeping and so they cant give good recomendations. Right now the
clinics mostly just ask the worker how they have been sleeping and the worker says fine or not
fine. This is not data driven and is a big gap in the market that nobody is addressing in a
meaningful way.
Our Solution
Sleepledger is a web app that collects sleep and schedule data from shift workers and gives it
to occupational clinics so they can recommend personalized rest plans and spot fatigue risks
early. The worker goes to the website and types in what time they went to sleep, what time they
woke up, and what shifts they worked. Our system then does analytics on the data and produces a
score for each worker. The clinic has a dashboard where they can see all of there workers and
who has a high score. Then the clinic can make a rest plan for the worker. We believe this is a
holistic end to end solution that leverages the power of data to transform how fatigue is
managed. Our prototype MVP has been built and has the worker log page and a basic clinic page.
Market Opportunity
The market for this is very large. There are many shift workers in the United States, probably
around 15 to 20 percent of all workers, which is tens of millions of people. There are also
thousands of occupational clinics. The sleep health market is growing every year and is
expected to be worth many billions of dollars. If we only capture a small percent of this
market we will be very succesful. We have not done a formal market study yet but we are
confident the numbers are big. Our target customers are occupational clinics first, and later
we may also go after employers, hospitals, trucking companies, and maybe insurance companies
and even individual consumers who want to track there sleep.
Business Model
Our business model has a few options and we are still deciding which is best. One option is
that clinics pay a monthly subscription for the dashboard. Another option is that workers pay a
small fee to use the app. A third option is that employers pay for the whole thing for there
workers. We might also sell the data and analytics to other companies, or charge for a
consulting service where we help clinics set up the rest plans. We think a mix of these will
work and will decide when we talk to more customers. Pricing has not been decided yet but it
would be somewhere between a low and medium price per month. Over time we expect revenue to
grow as more clinics and workers join the platform.
Competition
There are many sleep trackers and wearables on the market, as well as sleep apps, but these are
mostly for regular consumers and not for shift workers and clinics. Some big companies make
smart watches that track sleep automatically. We think we are different because we focus on
shift workers and clinics and combine the sleep with the work schedule. We do not think any
competitor does exactly what we do, although we have not searched very thoroughly. Our
advantage is that we understand the problem and are first to this specific niche. Large
companies could copy us, but we believe we can move faster because we are a small and agile

team.
Team
Brandon Teller is the CEO and is a senior at our university studying business. He came up with
the idea after his uncle, who is a night shift worker, said he was always tired. Brandon is in
charge of strategy, sales, and the vision of the company.
Kiara Oduya-Whitfield is the head of product and is a junior studying psychology with a minor
in health sciences. She has an interest in sleep and has read many articles about it. She is
responsible for the user experience and for the content of the rest plans.
Marcus Delvecchio is the CTO and is a sophomore studying computer science. He built the
prototype MVP over a few months and is responsible for the website and all the technical parts
including the analytics.
We do not currently have a clinician or a sleep doctor on the team, but we plan to find an
advisor in the future.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core business concept, formed our legal entity as an S Corp, built a
prototype MVP, and launched a website. We have not yet had any paying customers or any clinics
using the product. We have shown the prototype to a few friends and family members, who said it
looks good. We have not yet run a pilot. We have not yet had any revenue, and our expenses so
far have been small, mostly the cost of forming the company and the website hosting, which the
founders paid for themselves.
For financials, we project that in year one we will have a small number of clinics and some
revenue, and that by year three we will have grown to many clinics and be profitable. We have
not built a detailed financial model yet, but we believe the growth will be rapid because the
market is so big. Our main costs will be software development, marketing, and eventually hiring
staff. We expect to break even at some point once we have enough customers.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize money from the competition to help us take Sleepledger to the next
level. We would use the funds for further development of the product, marketing, and finding
our first clinic customers. We would also like to get mentorship and connections to people in
the health industry and investors, since we do not have much experience in healthcare. Any
amount would be helpful, but a larger amount would let us hire a developer and do a real pilot.
We also would like advice on privacy and regulation, since we know health data can be sensitive
and there are laws but we are not sure exactly which ones apply to us.
Conclusion
Sleepledger has the potential to change how fatigue is managed for shift workers everywhere.
With a huge market, a passionate team, and a working prototype, we believe we are well
positioned to succeed and to make a real difference in peoples lives. We thank the judges for
there time and consideration.
